title: Hyperbatch transpose race causing residual buffer desynchronization and softmax underflow drift
creator: Nadia Kim
description:
Summary:
A recent change to the multi-stream hyperbatch transpose optimization (introduced in runtime-1.21) appears to introduce a non-deterministic correctness regression. Under moderate concurrency (multiple prefill + decode streams), outputs exhibit token-order skew and low-amplitude numerical drift in softmax outputs that accumulates across long generations. In production this shows as hallucination-like shifts on long-context workloads and an increased tail latency variance.

Observed failure modes:
- Token order anomalies: rare off-by-one token insertion/deletion observed in ~0.3% of sampled requests for long sequence lengths (>2048) under 8+ concurrent streams.
- Softmax underflow drift: logits for later tokens show small but systematic negative bias compared to baseline, causing subtle changes in sampling probabilities (rarely changes top-1, often changes tail mass).
- Prefill/Decode interleaving corruption: in a few cases KV cache indices appear mismatched for a single stream after another stream prefilled a contiguous hyperbatch slice.

Reproduction steps (deterministic):
1) Checkout branch: main@runtime-1.21 (with hyperbatch transpose enabled).
2) Run synthetic harness: tests/synth/hyperbatch_long_context.py with SEED=4242, concurrent_streams=12, seq_len_prefill=4096, decode_len=512, model=redwood/gptX-30B-qat_fp16.
3) Compare token sequences and per-token logits against runtime-1.20 baseline (disable hyperbatch transpose).
4) Failure observed in 3/100 runs: token mismatch + KL divergence of per-token distribution > 1e-3 for tokens after position 1024.

Hypothesis / Root cause: 
During adaptive kernel selection we introduced a per-device transient buffer that stores transposed activation slabs for batched attention kernels. The buffer is multiplexed across streams using a lightweight epoch counter and a best-effort CAS, but the fast path omitted an atomic fence when swapping the residual/transposed pointer on fallback kernels. Under high concurrency a prefill thread can start using a slab still being torn down by a concurrent decode stream: this yields a temporal alias where accumulating FXP/FP16 reductions see partially-overwritten inputs. The corrupted inputs cause tiny rounding differences in softmax exponent accumulation; because we use mixed-precision accumulation (FP16 paths with FP32 accumulation in some kernels) the rounding bias is non-linear and propagates across attention windows, producing the observed drift. Additionally the per-stream KV-index update was not fully linearized with respect to the transpose buffer lifetime which explains occasional KV misindexing.

Mitigation applied (temporary):
- Disabled hyperbatch transpose fast-path on runtime-1.21 (hotfix branch) for loaded GPUs with >4 concurrent streams.
- Added a conservative memory fence + stream fence in the kernel handshake for the slab swap in hotfix.

Work done so far:
- Reproduced locally and in canary region (us-west-2) using production traffic replay; added token-level diff logging.
- Instrumented per-slab epoch counters and added histograms for slab-failures/ABA detections.
- Implemented two candidate fixes: 
  1) Fix A (safety-first): strong atomic swap + fence + single-producer lock per-slab. Deterministic, low risk, measurable overhead (~2-4% token cost on synthetic microbenchmarks).
  2) Fix B (perf-first): reordered pipeline to ensure slab lifetime extends until downstream decode commits KV-index (uses release-acquire semantics, avoids global lock). Lower overhead (<=1% median cost) but more complex and requires careful formalization of invariants.
- Added unit tests to reproduce ABA by injecting scheduler yields at the CAS point.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Is the small perf delta (1-2%) acceptable to keep Fix A as default? Fix A is simplest and easiest to backport. Fix B gives better perf but has a larger surface area and must be verified for all kernel variants (FP16, BF16, FP32) and hardware (A100, H100, gV100).
- We need to determine if mixed-precision accumulation policy should be made deterministic (always do FP32 accumulation for softmax reductions). That reduces drift but increases memory/compute cost.

Next steps / proposed plan:
1) Short term (this sprint): merge Fix A into runtime-1.21-hotfix and roll to 100% on Dedicated Canary group with traffic-sliced workloads. Monitor token-diff rate and tail error budget. (Assigned to Rafael)
2) Medium term: fully implement and stress-test Fix B on a hardware matrix in CI; add formal spec doc and code comments for handshake invariants. (Assigned to Nadia + Rafael pair)
3) Long term: evaluate moving to deterministic FP32 accumulation in attention inner-reduction or provide a toggle per-model/route in Redwood Console.

Monitoring / Metrics to watch:
- token-diff-rate (fraction of requests with any token mismatch) — alert threshold >0.01%
- per-token KL divergence averaged over last-token window of 256 tokens — alert >2e-4
- slab-ABA-histogram and CAS-retry-rate
- tail latency (p99.9) on prefill-heavy workloads

Artifacts / Links:
- Repro harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/tree/main/tests/synth/hyperbatch_long_context.py
- Canary dashboard (prod replay): https://dash.redwood.ai/d/rtc/hyperbatch-canary?orgId=1
- Hotfix branch PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/11458
- Fix B WIP PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/11492
- Investigation notes: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/1Hy_perfbatch_investigation

Acceptance criteria for closing:
- Hotfix deployed to all production fleets with token-diff-rate within baseline tolerance (<0.001%) for 72h of representative traffic AND
- Fix B validated in CI hardware matrix with no reproducible ABA failures under stress harness and benchmarked to show <1.5% median token-cost delta OR a design decision and rollout plan documented to prefer Fix A permanently.
